sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go maps support key-to-value lookup and are commonly used for sets, frequency counts, grouping, memoization, and complement searches. Keys must be comparable.

A set uses `map[T]struct{}`, a counter uses `map[T]int`, and the comma-ok form distinguishes an absent key from a present key holding its zero value.

For example, to find the first repeated number, check `seen[n]` before adding `n`. For word counts, increment `counts[word]`; a missing key naturally starts from integer zero.

Map iteration order is unspecified, and maps are not safe for unsynchronized concurrent read/write access. Expected constant-time operations do not remove the need to analyse memory growth.

Use a set for membership and a frequency table when duplicates matter. A map is especially valuable when the key range is large or unknown and direct array indexing is not practical.

sections.title: The core model: hash-map patterns in Go
sections.content:
hash-map patterns in Go is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

A map turns information from earlier input into direct later lookup. That is why the same structure solves apparently different problems: a set remembers existence, a counter remembers multiplicity, and a complement map remembers where a useful partner appeared. The value type is the state the algorithm needs.

sections.title: The practical decision: hash-map patterns in Go
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether hash-map patterns in Go can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

Use `struct{}` when presence is the only fact, `int` for counts or indexes, and a slice value for grouping several items per key. A fixed array can replace a map for a guaranteed small dense alphabet, but using it without that guarantee changes the accepted input.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: hash-map patterns in Go
sections.content:
Failures around hash-map patterns in Go usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

The zero-value read is convenient for `counts[key]++`, yet it can hide absence when zero is a valid stored value. The comma-ok result carries that missing bit. Nil maps are similarly asymmetric: reads are allowed, but the first assignment panics, so construction ownership must be clear.

sections.title: The important trade-off: hash-map patterns in Go
sections.content:
hash-map patterns in Go and repeated slice scans solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

Array indexing gives worst-case constant access with no hashing when a key maps safely into a bounded dense range. Maps support strings, structs of comparable fields, and sparse integers without reserving every possible slot. Their flexibility costs metadata, buckets, and less predictable locality.

A good investigation traces the first point where the real state differs from the expected state. With hash-map patterns in Go, that means observing the relevant input, transition, and result rather than guessing from the final symptom.

A map trace should state its invariant, such as 'contains values from indexes before i.' Recording state before and after insertion exposes self-matches and wrong update order.
